clips.title: The Browser is a very Confused Deputy - web 0x05
clips.why: The original confused deputy story, a compiler with two kinds of authority, which is exactly the trap a broker that only forwards falls into.
look: One program, authority from two sources: the user's request and its own rights. Our broker has the same two.
The definition: a deputy with power, tricked into using it for someone who should not have it.
Ask yourself while watching: what would the deputy have to check to stay safe?
clips.after: Our broker is a deputy with the GitHub key. Checking every request against the run's scope is what keeps it from being confused.

clips.title: The Browser is a very Confused Deputy - web 0x05
clips.why: The cure he points to is capability-based permissions: the request carries the authority, instead of the deputy using its own.
look: The server-side request forgery example: a server fetching a URL for a user, with the server's own access.
Capabilities: the right to do something travels with the request, so the deputy cannot be tricked into using more.
clips.after: Nova's capability is that idea: it carries exactly one run's rights, and the broker never uses more than the scope allows.

clips.title: GitHub Actions: GITHUB_TOKEN Explained | How it works, Change Permissions, Customizations
clips.why: A familiar example of a short-lived token made for one repository and one job, then thrown away.
look: The token is created for the run and expires when the job ends.
It works only for the repository the workflow runs in.
clips.after: The broker asks GitHub for the same kind of token for each run: one repo, one hour, and it never leaves the broker.

clips.title: GitHub Actions: GITHUB_TOKEN Explained | How it works, Change Permissions, Customizations
clips.why: Permissions can be listed one by one, so a token gets only what the job needs.
look: Each permission (contents, pull-requests, and so on) can be read, write or none.
Least privilege: ask for less, and a leak can do less.
clips.after: Our broker asks for contents and pull_requests write, checks and actions read, and never workflows.

practice.q: The broker receives a request with a capability whose scope expired ten minutes ago. What does it answer?

options.text: 401, as if the capability were unknown
options.why: An expired scope is treated like no scope. The run is over, so its capability means nothing.

options.text: 200, because the capability itself is still valid
options.why: A capability has no validity of its own; it is only a pointer to a scope, and the scope has ended.
The broker never gets that far: without a live scope, it does not know what the request may do.

practice.hint: The branch comes from the run's scope, never from the request.

practice.q: Put one push from Nova's VM in order.
items: git on the VM sends the push to the broker, with the capability from the credential helper
The broker hashes the capability and finds the run's scope
The broker reads the ref updates at the start of the push
The broker checks: own branch, no delete, branch not moved
The broker adds the one-hour token and sends the same bytes to GitHub
practice.why: The token is added last, only after every check passed, and it never travels back to the VM.

practice.q: Which of these makes the broker a confused deputy?

options.text: It forwards a push to main because the request carried a valid capability
options.why: A valid capability says who is asking, not that this request is allowed. The scope must be checked too.

options.text: It refuses a push to main and writes REFUSED in the audit log
options.why: That is the broker doing its job.

options.text: It asks GitHub for a new token every 50 minutes
options.why: Refreshing a short token is normal; it gives the run no more power.

practice.q: A ref update deletes the branch when its new commit is
practice.hint: The length of a SHA-1 commit ID in hex.
practice.why: Git sends a new commit of forty zeros to mean "delete this ref", and the broker refuses it.
